steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Conceptual tour of a Transformer

1. Core idea  
   Treat every element of a sequence (a word-piece, a pixel patch, an audio frame, …) as a vector that is free to look at every other element through “attention.” Instead of walking left-to-right like an RNN or sliding a window like a CNN, the model repeatedly asks, for each position:  
   “Which other positions are relevant to me, and by how much?”  
   These relevance scores (attention weights) are learned and updated layer after layer, so increasingly rich, context-aware representations emerge.

2. Input → vectors + order information  
   • Token embedding: a learned lookup converts each discrete token id into a dense vector.  
   • Positional encoding: because attention itself is permutation-invariant, we inject “where this token sits” by adding or concatenating a position vector (sine/cosine pattern or a learned table).  
   Result: a sequence of d-dimensional vectors X = (x₁ … xₙ).

3. Self-attention (one head)  
   From each xᵢ two questions and one answer are produced through learned linear maps:  
   Query  qᵢ = W_Q xᵢ  (What am I looking for?)  
   Key    kᵢ = W_K xᵢ  (What do I contain that others may want?)  
   Value  vᵢ = W_V xᵢ  (What information can I give if I’m selected?)  

   To build an updated representation for position i:  
      scoreᵢⱼ = (qᵢ · kⱼ) / √d   (similarity, scaled)  
      αᵢⱼ    = softmaxⱼ(scoreᵢⱼ)  (normalize across j)  
      zᵢ      = Σⱼ αᵢⱼ vⱼ         (weighted mixture of values)  

   Visually, each row of the α matrix is a “heat-map” of which tokens position i attends to.

4. Multi-head attention  
   Instead of one set (Q,K,V) we use h of them in parallel (different weight matrices). Each head captures different kinds of relationships (syntax, long-distance coreference, positional offsets, …). Heads are concatenated and linearly remixed.

5. Add & Norm  
   The attention output is added back to the input (residual connection) and layer-normalized. This stabilizes training and lets deeper stacks form.

6. Position-wise feed-forward network (FFN)  
   A two-layer MLP applied independently to every position:  
   FFN(x) = W₂ ReLU(W₁x) (or GELU).  
   Again, residual + layer norm. This gives the model non-linear capacity that is not purely based on pairwise interactions.

7. Stack L identical blocks → the Encoder  
   The encoder turns raw token vectors into contextual vectors that “know about” the whole sentence/document.

8. Decoder (for sequence generation tasks)  
   Another stack, but each block contains:  
   a) Masked self-attention (looks only at earlier positions so generation is causal).  
   b) Encoder-decoder attention (the decoder queries the encoder’s output, so it can “peek” at the source sentence in translation or the image in captioning).  
   c) FFN + residual + norm.  
   The final decoder vector at step t is passed through a linear layer + softmax to produce a probability distribution for the next token.

9. Training  
   • Objective: maximize likelihood of correct next token (cross-entropy).  
   • Teacher forcing: ground-truth previous tokens are fed in.  
   • Large-scale pre-training (masked-LM, next-token, etc.) followed by task-specific fine-tuning is common.

10. Why it works  
    • Global connectivity: any token can interact with any other in one hop → captures long-range dependencies without vanishing gradients.  
    • Parallelism: no recurrence; whole sequence processed simultaneously → efficient on GPUs/TPUs.  
    • Expressiveness: multiple heads and deep stacking let the model learn layered abstractions (syntax → semantics → domain knowledge).  
    • Flexibility: same architecture scales from thousands to hundreds of billions of parameters and adapts to text, images, audio, proteins, code.

11. Mental picture  
    Imagine a round-table discussion held repeatedly: at each layer every word listens to all other words, decides whose statements are relevant, then re-says itself enriched by what it heard. After several rounds, each word’s vector encapsulates the gist of the whole conversation from its own perspective. The decoder then “speaks” the sequence aloud, one token at a time, using what the encoder discussed.

That’s the conceptual essence: attention-based interaction + feed-forward processing, stacked deep, with position cues and residual normalization glue—the Transformer.
